title: GB vs GiB, MB vs MiB: The 4.9% Storage Discrepancy
h1: Storage capacity units — GB (SI) vs GiB (IEC)
description: 1 GB = 10⁹ bytes (SI). 1 GiB = 2³⁰ = 1.074 × 10⁹ bytes (IEC). Drive manufacturers use SI; operating systems mostly show IEC. The 7% gap is why 'my 1 TB drive shows as 931 GB'.

author.name: The Turbo Unit Converter engineering desk

reviewer.name: Turbo Unit Converter editorial review
reviewer.credential: verified against NIST SP 811 and category-specific ISO references

hero: SI multiplies by 1000. IEC binary multiplies by 1024. Everyone kept using GB, MB but pointing at different powers.
body: Storage capacity notation has been ambiguous since the 1970s. Manufacturers report decimal multiples (GB = 10⁹ B). OS tools historically use binary multiples but keep the SI label. The IEC standardised the binary prefixes (Ki, Mi, Gi) in 1999 but adoption remains partial.

> Decimal (SI): 1 kB = 10³ B, 1 MB = 10⁶ B, 1 GB = 10⁹ B, 1 TB = 10¹² B
> Binary (IEC): 1 KiB = 2¹⁰ = 1024 B, 1 MiB = 2²⁰, 1 GiB = 2³⁰, 1 TiB = 2⁴⁰
> 1 GiB / 1 GB = 1.0737 (7.4% larger); grows to 10% at TB scale

Decimal (GB, TB): storage drive marketing, network throughput, some file managers (macOS since 10.6). Binary (GiB, TiB): most Linux tools, Windows Explorer, RAM capacity (always binary because address lines are powers of 2).
A '1 TB' drive holds 10¹² bytes = 9.31 × 10¹¹ / 1024⁴ = 931 GiB. Windows shows 931 GB (labelled GB but computed as GiB). Neither is wrong — they use different definitions of the same abbreviation.

faqs.a: Memory address lines are natively powers of 2. A 4 GiB DIMM has exactly 4 × 2³⁰ bytes; there is no decimal equivalent.

faqs.q: Is network throughput SI or binary?
faqs.a: Almost always SI. '1 Gbps' = 10⁹ bits per second, not 2³⁰.
